The strongest surviving evidence places “night names” within trade and the effort to connect traders with official household records. Deliberate resistance remains a plausible use, but it is less securely established as the original or chief purpose. The archive supports an unevenly weighted account of several functions, not a verdict about what all residents intended.

## The strongest evidence concerns practical use and official recording

The harbor register shows that short names were added beside 19 of 62 surviving trader entries. Thirteen of those 19 traders operated boats after dusk, linking the recorded practice with nighttime trade. The other six lack recorded boat occupations; that is not evidence that they never worked on boats. Because the register concerns taxable movements, its entries show what officials recorded, not the full range of names people used privately. [B05-S1]

The marginal note suggests a distinction between a short name used around the tides and a household identity answerable for tax. However, the annotations are undated, and the note may not be by the person who added the names. We cannot confidently combine them into one dated administrative policy. Nor does official recording establish that officials invented the names. [B05-S1]

The letter dated year 44 provides the clearest statement of a practical aim: four traders wanted faster clearance and asked the clerk to keep both names. Its account describes a mismatch between what inspectors requested and what boatmen supplied. Three signatories match annotated register entries, strengthening the connection between the two documents and particular traders. It does not establish when those annotations were made, and the fourth trader's missing entry cannot be treated as evidence of an exception to the practice. [B05-S2]

The letter supports the petitioners' stated wish to reconcile names for administrative purposes. It does not directly show that night names were originally created to make trading easier: in the situation described, the mismatch was slowing trade. Its survival through an official copy also matters. Confrontational wording could have been softened, as one historian proposes, but no alternative version establishes that this happened. A possible alteration cannot be used as evidence for the missing words. [B05-S2]

## Resistance is suggested by a later, less secure account

The former watch officer's memoir describes night names as frustrating arrest and making official ledgers objects of mockery. If accurate, it would support a use that obstructed authority and, at least among some people, a defiant attitude. But the memoir was written in year 79 about year 43, a gap of 36 years. The author's admitted confusion about flood seasons raises a specific concern about remembered chronology. Its sale during a campaign against a new tax authority also gives reason to consider how the past was selected and presented for a later audience. Neither issue automatically makes the account false. [B05-S3]

The verified gate descriptions establish accuracy about those geographical details. They do not independently confirm the naming story or traders' motives. Corroboration is strongest when it checks the claim under dispute; accuracy elsewhere cannot do that work. [B05-S3]

The song offers still less direct evidence about a historical policy or widespread intention. Its language is compatible with retaining more than one identity, but poetry cannot simply be read as a register of actual behavior. The year 88 date belongs to the surviving copy, not necessarily the composition. The collector's resistance heading is a later interpretation, weakened further by the inclusion of unrelated wedding verses. The year 112 catalog's claim that citizens abandoned household identities goes beyond the fragment, which does not say one name replaced the other. [B05-S4]

## Functions, intentions, and later meanings can differ

A name could work conveniently among boatmen while causing difficulty when an inspector tried to connect it to a taxable household. That difficulty would be an effect of the practice; it would not by itself prove that evading officials was why the name was adopted. Conversely, a request to record both names shows the signatories' practical goal at that moment, without ruling out political intentions among other users—or other motives among the same users.

The best-supported synthesis is therefore that some traders used alternative names, officials encountered problems connecting those names with household identities, and at least four traders sought a practical arrangement that retained both. Official annotations show some incorporation into records, although their timing and relationship to the petition remain uncertain. Later sources gave the practice an explicit association with conflict over authority. Earlier practical uses and later political meanings could coexist; one need not erase the other. [B05-S1–S4]

One live alternative is that some night names were deliberately used to obscure household connections and resist enforcement from an early stage. The memoir is consistent with that possibility, and practical petitions would not exclude it. But making resistance the chief original purpose would require stronger contemporary evidence of intent. The unverified suggestion that the official copy softened the letter cannot supply that evidence.

## What the museum should leave open

The 19 annotations among 62 surviving entries describe this incomplete register, not the prevalence of night names among all traders or residents. Missing pages, selective recording, and the archive's focus on taxable activity prevent that extrapolation. The register's year 41 date does not date later annotations; the letter and memoir do not establish the practice's origin; and the song's copy date cannot establish when it was composed. [B05-S1–S4]

Finally, the documents do not establish one shared motive, an organized movement, a formal town-wide naming policy, or widespread abandonment of household identities. A museum label can confidently present trade and administrative reconciliation as the best-attested setting, identify resistance as a plausible but less securely documented use, and show how later writers made the practice politically meaningful without claiming that later interpretation settles its beginnings.

这次事件表明：**当前网关允许同一个有效请求在时间窗口内再次通过，而订单服务确实为这两次提交创建了两个订单。** 这不说明 HMAC 被破解。签名保护了请求中的 tenant 路径，但不能赋予客户端该 tenant 的成员资格；是否有权创建订单，仍由服务判断。

## 先分清三个问题

- **认证**：请求对应哪个客户端账户，签名覆盖的内容是否与签名一致。当前网关使用 `HMAC_SHA256`，签名覆盖 `method`、`path`、`timestamp` 和 `SHA256(body_bytes)`；识别密钥后，转发请求并添加 `X-Client-ID`。
- **授权**：这个账户是否有权在目标 tenant 执行操作。订单服务通过 `directory.is_member(client, tenant)` 检查成员资格。
- **防重放**：已经有效提交过的请求再次到达时，是否会被再次接受或执行。版本 3 没有 nonce store，即没有保存已使用请求标记的机制，也没有承诺最多执行一次。

`timestamp` 必须在网关时间的 60 秒范围内，只限制请求的时间窗口，并不标识“这是一个从未处理过的操作”。同一个请求可以在窗口内到达多次；不同请求也可以使用同一个时间戳。所有涉事密钥都允许 `POST`，所以方法限制不是本次拒绝 T2 请求的原因。[B06-S1–S2]

## 每次响应分别说明什么

| 时间与请求 | 观察结果 | 能得出的结论 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10:00:08，提交在 10:00:00 签名的 `POST /tenants/T1/orders` | 网关接受，服务返回 `201` | 请求通过认证，K 通过 T1 成员检查，服务执行了创建流程 |
| 10:00:15，完全相同的重试 | 再次返回 `201` | 原签名仍在时间窗口内；当前处理流程没有把这次重试复用为第一次操作的结果 |
| 10:00:20，只把捕获请求的路径改为 `/tenants/T2/orders` | 网关在转发前拒绝 | 修改了签名覆盖的 `path`，却没有重新计算签名，因此请求无法通过认证 |
| 10:00:25，K 用合法密钥为 T2 路径计算有效签名 | 网关接受，服务返回 `403` | K 可以证明自己的客户端身份，但仍不是 T2 成员，授权检查阻止了创建 |

前两次 `201` 加上存储日志，才构成这次重复创建的完整证据：T1 中存在两个不同订单标识，二者的 `reference` 都是 R7。第一次响应连接失败，表示客户端没有可靠收到结果，不能据此认定第一次订单没有保存。重试到达时，代码再次运行到 `save_order(tenant, order)`。[B06-S2–S3]

10:00:20 的拒绝发生在网关，因此它证明的是本次路径篡改未通过签名检查，并不是服务完成了一次 T2 成员检查。10:00:25 则把两个层次分开了：签名有效，网关接受；成员资格不满足，服务返回 `403`，不会运行后面的 `save_order(tenant, order)`。[B06-S2–S3]

所以，“签名包含 tenant”意味着这个路径不能在不重新签名的情况下被替换。它不意味着持有密钥的人可以为自己选择任意 tenant 权限。K 能签署自己的请求，也能签署一个自己无权执行的请求。

## 哪份文档适用于这次事件

应按当前版本 3 解释行为。版本 1 中“签名请求不能重复”的说法依赖 nonce 数据库，而该机制已经从版本 3 移除。不能把旧机制的承诺保留在对当前系统的判断中。[B06-S1, B06-S4]

“有效签名授予访问”的幻灯片省略了服务授权这一层，不能覆盖当前合同对服务职责的明确规定。99.99 percent availability 衡量的是网关可用性，不能证明授权正确、没有重复订单，或请求只执行一次。[B06-S4]

## tenant 授权继续放在订单服务执行

在题设部署中，服务只能通过网关访问，并读取网关添加的 `X-Client-ID`。服务应结合这个客户端身份和路径中的 `tenant`，在创建订单前执行成员资格及相关资源权限检查。这与版本 3 的职责划分一致，也解释了 K 的有效 T2 签名为何最终得到 `403`。[B06-S1–S2]

给出的代码显示了成员检查，不能据此声称所有可能需要的资源权限检查都已实现。网关负责认证，并不替代服务对具体操作的授权。

## 建议增加按业务操作识别重试的设计

目标应是：客户端在响应丢失后，可以重试并取得第一次创建的结果，而不是再创建一个订单。这种“多次请求对应同一次业务效果”的性质叫作幂等性。下面是拟议变更，当前代码尚未提供这些机制。

1. **为创建操作生成稳定标识。** 客户端在第一次提交前生成并保存一个 `operation_id`，将它作为新增字段放入请求正文。所有重试沿用该值和相同的订单内容。放在正文中的标识会随 `body_bytes` 一起受到现有签名公式保护。不能直接假定 `order.reference` 全局唯一；若要用它作为业务唯一标识，必须先明确唯一性的适用范围和业务规则。

2. **服务在认证、授权之后查找该操作。** 保存操作记录时，范围至少包括客户端、tenant 和创建订单这一操作类型，并绑定请求内容的摘要。同一范围内，相同 `operation_id` 和相同内容应取得已保存的结果；相同标识配上不同内容应被拒绝，不能悄悄创建另一张订单。

3. **把“占用操作标识、创建订单、保存结果”做成一个可靠的整体。** 例如，在同一数据库事务中完成，并对操作标识设置唯一约束。这样两个并发重试不会都发现“还没有记录”后各自创建订单；也不会出现订单已经提交、去重记录却未保存的空隙。若首次操作仍在处理中，后来的请求应等待或得到可查询的处理中状态，而不是再调用创建流程。

4. **重试返回原操作的结果。** 为成功操作保存状态码和响应内容，新方案可在响应中包含原订单标识。客户端即使错过第一次响应，重试也能得到同一订单的结果。超过认证时间窗口后，客户端可以用新 `timestamp` 重新计算签名，但必须保留原 `operation_id`；新的签名不能被当成新的业务操作。

5. **明确记录保留期和过期后的行为。** 操作记录至少要覆盖承诺支持的重试期限。记录删除后若允许同一标识再次创建，就不能继续承诺任意久之后的重试也只产生一次效果。要提供更长保证，就需要相应的持久记录或明确拒绝过期重试。

全局拒绝每个重复签名只能阻止部分字节完全相同的重放，不能让丢失响应的客户端取回原结果。它也不能识别“同一业务操作换了时间戳并重新签名”的重试。因此，需要围绕业务操作保存和复用结果，而不能把签名或时间戳直接当作订单操作标识。

## 这次证据的边界

日志证明了这两次提交产生了两个订单；它们不提供重复订单的总体发生率。代码没有展示 `order.reference` 唯一性检查、幂等键处理或重复提交间共享的事务标识；本次日志也表明，`save_order` 没有把这两次提交合并成一张订单。但不能据此编造它在其他输入下的任何未公开行为。[B06-S2–S3]

路径篡改被拒绝、合法签名的越权请求被服务拒绝，都与当前合同一致。这些观察没有显示 HMAC 被破解，也不是对所有可能攻击的全面验证。它们足以定位本次问题：当前认证和成员授权不能提供业务操作的重试去重保证，而版本 3 本来就没有承诺这种保证。

HeatNest erzeugt nach diesen Messungen keine Energie. Das Verhältnis vier zu eins stimmt für die Entladephase, berücksichtigt aber nicht die gleichzeitig verbrauchte Speicherenergie. Über Entladen und Wiederaufladen zusammen beträgt der Nutzungsgrad an der **Apparategrenze rund 72,7 Prozent**.

## Leistung und Energie unterscheiden

**kW beschreibt Leistung:** wie schnell Energie übertragen wird. **kWh beschreibt eine Energiemenge.** Bei einer mittleren Leistung von 2 kW über 10 Stunden werden 20 kWh übertragen. Die folgenden Rechnungen beziehen sich zunächst auf den Apparat einschließlich Umwandler und Speicher, ohne Überwachungscomputer. Als nützlich zählt hier ausschließlich Wärme für den Demonstrationsraum. [B07-S1]

| Phase | Elektrische Energie hinein | Wärme in den Raum | Wärme in den Flur | Änderung der Speicherenergie |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Entladen, 10 Stunden | 2 kW × 10 h = 20 kWh | 8 kW × 10 h = 80 kWh | 10 kWh | −70 kWh |
| Aufladen, 5 Stunden | 18 kW × 5 h = 90 kWh | 0 kWh | 20 kWh | +70 kWh |
| Vollständiger Zyklus | 110 kWh | 80 kWh | 30 kWh | 0 kWh |

Die Werte stammen aus den beiden vollständig gemessenen Phasen. [B07-S2–S3]

## Warum vier zu eins keine Energieerzeugung bedeutet

Beim Entladen gilt:

\[
20\,\text{kWh Strom}+70\,\text{kWh Speicherabnahme}
=80\,\text{kWh Raumwärme}+10\,\text{kWh Flurwärme}.
\]

Das Verhältnis der mittleren Leistungen ist tatsächlich 8 kW / 2 kW = 4. Weil beide Mittelwerte dieselben zehn Stunden betreffen, gilt auch 80 kWh / 20 kWh = 4. Diese Kennzahl beschreibt die Raumwärme im Verhältnis zum Stromverbrauch **während der Entladung**. Sie ist kein Gesamtwirkungsgrad: Der Speicher liefert zusätzlich zuvor eingelagerte Energie, deren früherer Ladeverbrauch in diesem Stromzählerstand fehlt. Die Bezeichnung „vierhundert Prozent Gesamtwirkungsgrad“ verwechselt diese unterschiedlichen Bezugsgrößen. [B07-S2]

Auch der erste Kritiker irrt: Energieerhaltung verbietet keine Wärmeabgabe oberhalb der gleichzeitigen elektrischen Aufnahme, wenn dabei gespeicherte Energie abnimmt. Umgekehrt erklärt die Speicherabnahme allein die Raumwärme ebenfalls nicht: 70 kWh sind weniger als 80 kWh. Die 20 kWh elektrische Aufnahme gehören zur Bilanz. Wie genau beide Beiträge auf Raum- und Flurwärme verteilt werden, lässt sich aus diesen Gesamtmessungen nicht vollständig bestimmen.

Bezieht man die Raumwärme beim Entladen auf die gesamte verfügbare Energie aus Strom und Speicherabnahme, ergibt sich 80 / (20 + 70) ≈ 88,9 Prozent. Auch das ist eine Kennzahl nur dieser Phase; sie enthält die Ladeverluste noch nicht.

## Der vollständige Zyklus

Beim Wiederaufladen lautet die Bilanz:

\[
90\,\text{kWh Strom}=70\,\text{kWh Speicherzuwachs}+20\,\text{kWh Flurwärme}.
\]

Damit sind 70 / 90 ≈ 77,8 Prozent des Ladestroms als zusätzliche Speicherenergie vorhanden. Nach beiden Phasen hat der Speicher wieder seinen Anfangszustand. Deshalb lässt sich die Nutzenergie jetzt ohne einen verbleibenden Speicherbeitrag mit dem gesamten Stromverbrauch vergleichen:

\[
\eta_{\text{Apparat}}=
\frac{80\,\text{kWh}}{20\,\text{kWh}+90\,\text{kWh}}
\approx72{,}7\,\%.
\]

Die übrigen 30 kWh gingen in den Flur. Das Aufladen als „Wartung“ zu bezeichnen ändert seine notwendige Rolle nicht: Ohne Wiederherstellung des Speichers kann die nächste identische Entladung nicht beginnen. 2 kW direkt zu 90 kWh zu addieren wäre dagegen ein Einheitenfehler; zunächst müssen die 2 kW über zehn Stunden in 20 kWh umgerechnet werden. [B07-S3–S4]

## Größere Grenze und anderer Nutzen

An der **Installationsgrenze einschließlich Überwachungscomputer** kommen 3 kWh Verbrauch hinzu, ohne zusätzliche Raumwärme. Der Nutzungsgrad sinkt auf 80 / 113 ≈ **70,8 Prozent**. Der Energieverbleib beim Computer müsste in einer vollständigen Installationsbilanz ebenfalls erfasst werden; diese 3 kWh dürfen nicht der Raumwärme zugerechnet werden. [B07-S1]

„Nützlich“ hängt vom erklärten Zweck ab. Für diese Demonstration bleiben die 30 kWh Flurwärme Verluste. Wollte ein anderer Kunde tatsächlich Raum und Flur mit genau dieser Wärme versorgen, könnten beide Ausgänge als Nutzen zählen: Dann wären es an der Apparategrenze 110 / 110 = 100 Prozent. Das wäre eine andere Nutzenbewertung derselben physikalischen Bilanz, keine zusätzliche Energie. Sie müsste ausdrücklich angegeben werden. Der Designpreis belegt keinen Wirkungsgrad, und die Messungen belegen keine Leistung unter anderen Betriebsbedingungen. [B07-S1, B07-S4]

The low reported latency and the large backlog describe different populations. The latency histogram describes jobs that finished; the unfinished-job gauge also includes jobs that remained stuck. The supplied figures do **not** justify doubling the workers: dependency blocking is a credible cause, and worker capacity has not been established as the limiting factor.

## What the counts establish

The flow balance is exact:

\[
120\text{ initially unfinished}+600\text{ admitted}-540\text{ completed}
=180\text{ finally unfinished}.
\]

Over 600 seconds, the admission rate was **1 job/second**, the completion rate was **0.9 jobs/second**, and unfinished work increased by 60 jobs, averaging **0.1 job/second**. Calling 540 / 600 the arrival rate confuses completions with admissions. The measured mean of 150 unfinished jobs includes waiting, executing, and dependency-blocked jobs; it does not mean that 150 workers were occupied. [B08-S1, B08-S3]

## Why the latency statistics can stay low

The mean of 20 seconds and the ninety-fifth percentile of 25 seconds concern the **540 completed jobs**. Their durations run from original admission to completion, even where admission preceded this window. Roughly 95 percent of that completed-job sample finished within 25 seconds, subject to the percentile convention. This says neither that 95 percent of the 600 new admissions finished that quickly nor that 95 percent of all jobs present did. The 180 unfinished jobs are absent from the histogram. [B08-S2]

If one class continues normally while another waits indefinitely for a dependency, the normal jobs keep supplying short completed durations. The stalled jobs keep increasing the unfinished count and their own ages without contributing a completed duration. That mechanism fits the reported dependency interruption, although the missing class labels prevent us from identifying every stuck job. [B08-S3]

## Why the average-work relationship does not resolve this window

The relationship usually called Little’s law connects long-run average jobs present, admission rate, and total time per job for the **same system and population**, under conditions where those averages exist and work does not accumulate without bound. It does not require all jobs to behave alike, but applying it to short-window measurements requires care about jobs crossing the window boundaries.

Here, the gauge counts each job only for the portion of its lifetime inside the ten-minute window. The histogram instead counts the full lifetimes of completers and none of the unfinished lifetimes. Those are different accounting rules. Some jobs were already present at the start; others remain at the end. Consequently, multiplying 1 job/second by the completers’ 20-second mean is not a valid prediction of this window’s mean unfinished count. Likewise, 150 / 1 = 150 seconds is not a directly measured mean lifetime of the admitted jobs.

The summaries also impose a useful quantitative constraint; they do not permit just any explanation:

- The gauge represents 150 × 600 = **90,000 job-seconds** spent unfinished inside the window.
- All completed jobs’ full lifetimes together total 540 × 20 = **10,800 job-seconds**. Their contribution inside the window cannot exceed that total.
- Therefore, the 180 jobs unfinished at the end contributed **at least 79,200 job-seconds**, averaging at least **440 seconds each inside this window**.

Thus the unfinished jobs must account for most of the measured occupancy. They cannot all have arrived near the end. Any time completers spent before the window makes that lower bound larger. This explains how the instruments can agree without proving that either instrument is correct in every detail. [B08-S1–S2]

## What a scaling decision needs

Forty configured workers and 22 percent average CPU utilization do not establish a worker shortage. They also do not rule out a shortage affecting a particular worker pool or job class. Because execution slots can be released during external waits, unfinished-job count cannot substitute for occupied-slot count. Adding workers will not itself make an unresponsive dependency respond and could increase pressure on it. [B08-S3]

The most useful additional measurements are:

1. **Where jobs are waiting, split by class:** counts and ages for jobs awaiting a worker, executing, and awaiting the dependency, including the oldest unfinished jobs. Follow admission cohorts through completion so stuck jobs remain visible.
2. **Actual worker capacity:** occupied execution slots, runnable jobs waiting for slots, per-pool utilization, and execution time. This distinguishes unavailable workers from released slots and external waiting.
3. **Dependency behavior:** latency, outstanding requests, timeouts, errors, and rate limits, linked to job class. Compare these with changes in the incoming and unfinished workload mix.

Use that evidence to decide whether more workers can increase useful completions; a limited scaling trial can then test the proposed bottleneck.

Finally, 180 / 0.9 = **200 seconds** is a conditional drain estimate after admissions stop, assuming the same completion rate can be sustained until every remaining job finishes. It is not an exact forecast: the remaining jobs may be disproportionately blocked, and throughput may fall as the queue drains. The quarterly uptime statement supplies no missing evidence about this backlog or completion-time distribution. [B08-S4]

The passage makes Mara’s responsibility uncertain by showing how an accusation is assembled from evidence that will not quite support it. Its strongest implication is that the narrator wants to isolate Mara’s guilt while avoiding a more shared responsibility. But the narrator’s later exposure of that desire still does not establish who turned the wheel, what Mara authorized, or whether either person could have prevented harm.

## A memory organized around innocence

The opening reverses the expected order of reasoning: “I remember the gate opening because I remember being innocent.” Innocence appears to authorize the memory before the remembered event has been examined. The narrator sounds certain about a verdict while immediately becoming uncertain about the bell. The qualification “unless” and the possible “bell before the bell” unsettle the sequence on which judgments about warning and responsibility might depend. [B09-S1]

The missing boat repeats this pattern. Its absence becomes “proof” that the brother escaped, although it could support other possibilities. The retrospective admission that the narrator once “called many absences proof” invites distrust of the earlier reasoning. It also gives the older narrator an appearance of candor. That candor may help us recognize self-deception; it does not independently verify the corrected account or establish the brother’s fate.

The final movement separates clock time from remembered significance. The records place the opening at noon; memory places it at Mara’s withdrawal from conversation. The second account makes an event in their relationship into the event’s defining time. Neither account supplies the crucial sequence involving the shouting below. A record can give a precise time without answering who acted or what anyone knew. [B09-S3]

## Objects that invite accusation and then frustrate it

The key initially seems to assign control to Mara, but her reply redirects attention to the narrator’s empty belt and repeated reaching. The gesture could suggest habit, anxiety, or concealed involvement; it does not prove possession of the key. Similarly, hidden hands encourage suspicion before any action is seen. When Mara reveals a red palm, the wheel’s color makes contact seem possible, but the festival’s red handles supply other possible sources. The narrator’s sentence “I wanted the color to be an accusation” establishes that wish more securely than it establishes Mara’s act. [B09-S1–S2]

Other objects sharpen the difference between seeing and understanding. The water resembles an unopened letter: it can suggest significance awaiting recognition without telling us what anyone actually knew. The keeper’s lantern, lit or carried in daylight, adds no visibility. It may evoke the appearance of inspection or authority without additional evidence. The draft instruction to keep it unnecessary supports the deliberate preservation of that uselessness, not one compulsory symbolic meaning. [B09-S1–S2, B09-S4]

## Three questions of responsibility

The passage keeps distinct questions close enough that a reader can easily confuse them:

- **Physical action:** Who actually opened the gate? The final text does not say.
- **Authorization:** Who requested its opening? “She did” and “We did” offer competing accounts. Mara’s answer asserts shared involvement, but it remains testimony, not independent confirmation.
- **Warning:** Who knew the lower houses were at risk, and who could or should have warned them? The keeper’s question redirects attention toward this possible failure without establishing its circumstances. [B09-S2]

The keeper asks who *asked* for the gate, not who turned the wheel, and writes down neither answer. The scene therefore produces no official resolution of even the authorization dispute. Meanwhile, the narrator finds Mara’s hand easier to examine than the path toward the houses. That preference suggests an evasion of consequences: looking for a culprit can displace looking toward those who may have been harmed. It does not prove that a timely warning was possible.

## What the clearer notice leaves behind

“No one opens this gate alone” can function as an operating instruction, but its wording also allows a broader demand: opening the gate involves shared authorization, vigilance, or responsibility. “Two witnesses required” supplies a countable procedure. Witnessing an action, however, need not mean authorizing it, helping to assess its consequences, or ensuring that houses have been warned. The new wording can therefore make compliance clearer while narrowing the older notice’s moral reach. The passage does not show whether it improves actual safety. [B09-S3]

The narrator’s later position as keeper joins personal memory to institutional authority. Public praise rewards the revised notice; the old board remains privately preserved, turned away, and imagined in Mara’s voice. That combination suggests an unresolved demand beneath the successful clarification. Keeping the board could express attachment or guilt, but neither interpretation is a factual confession of a particular act.

The discarded sentence “Mara turned the wheel” shows that an earlier version resolved physical agency. Its omission matters precisely because that resolution is unavailable in the final text. The jacket’s “confession of a coward” is a later marketing interpretation, not external narrative evidence. Likewise, calling a red palm a universal code for guilt ignores the passage’s explicit alternative explanation. [B09-S4]

A leading reading is therefore that the narrator’s attempt to make Mara solely responsible exposes a possible shared failure instead. What resists a final verdict is specific: we still lack confirmation of the operator, the request, the brother’s fate, and the timing and possibility of warning. The uncertainty concerns how responsibility should be assigned as well as what happened.

Both presentations can contain correct percentages while drawing incorrect conclusions. Success rose within each recorded difficulty group, but the accepted workload shifted strongly toward Hard requests, whose success rate remained much lower. That shift lowered the overall rate. These comparisons describe the two periods; they do not isolate the tool’s effect or establish fairness between districts.

## The arithmetic and the changing mix

| Accepted requests | Baseline | Tool period | Change in success rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Easy | 90 / 100 = 90% | 19 / 20 = 95% | +5 percentage points |
| Hard | 20 / 100 = 20% | 60 / 200 = 30% | +10 percentage points |
| All | 110 / 200 = 55% | 79 / 220 ≈ 35.9% | −19.1 percentage points |

These denominators contain only accepted requests, all with complete seven-day outcomes. [B10-S1]

The baseline mix was half Easy and half Hard. In the tool period, only 20 / 220 ≈ 9.1% were Easy, while 90.9% were Hard. The overall rate is an average weighted by these shares. Although Hard performance improved to 30%, that rate remained far below Easy performance at 95%. Giving Hard requests much more weight pulled down the combined result.

This reversal between within-group and pooled comparisons is often called **Simpson’s paradox**. There is no arithmetic contradiction: the comparisons use different mixes. The first presentation is wrong that subgroup improvements force the overall rate upward. The second is wrong that an overall decline proves harm to every type of customer; both reported subgroup rates increased, and neither those increases nor the pooled decline establish individual causal effects. [B10-S3]

## What reweighting answers

Applying the tool-period rates to the baseline’s fifty-fifty mix gives:

\[
0.5(95\%)+0.5(30\%)=62.5\%.
\]

That is **7.5 percentage points above** the baseline’s 55%. It answers: “What weighted rate results if we hold the Easy/Hard shares at their baseline values and use the observed tool-period rates?” This is **descriptive standardization**: making the category weights comparable.

It does not establish that the tool caused a 7.5-point benefit. Training changed at the same time; the new contract changed acceptance; managers made undocumented overrides; and there was no concurrent untreated comparison or random assignment. Even within Hard, the accepted cases could have different unrecorded severity. Fixed category definitions prevent relabeling from explaining the result, but they do not make the cases otherwise equivalent. The 62.5% figure is also based on observed sample rates, including only 20 Easy requests in the tool period. [B10-S1–S3]

## Customer outcomes and district fairness remain separate questions

The reported metric asks whether an **accepted** request met a seven-day deadline. A later satisfactory repair still fails that metric. There were 110 recorded timely completions in the baseline period and 79 in the tool period; these are counts, not necessarily comparable rates per unit of calendar time. They do not count all eventual successful repairs. [B10-S1]

We cannot determine outcomes for incoming customers as a whole because rejected and abandoned requests were not retained. Nor can we infer how much unmet demand existed. Waiting before acceptance, eventual repairs, and access to the promise can change without being captured by the accepted-request success percentage. [B10-S2, B10-S4]

Nothing supplied establishes an East–West difference. Even equal success rates among accepted requests would not prove comparable access: selection can leave similar-looking accepted groups after very different admission decisions. The district field makes a future analysis possible; it supplies no missing cross-tabulation here. [B10-S4]

## A defensible evaluation

First, record **every incoming request**, including its district, predecision repair characteristics, tool recommendation, acceptance or rejection, override reason, abandonment, and relevant timestamps. Follow outcomes long enough to distinguish seven-day completion from later successful repair. Record unknown outcomes explicitly rather than treating missing follow-up as success.

Second, make the district comparison explicit. Agree in advance which predecision features—such as repair type, severity, and urgency—make requests comparable. Within those groups, compare East and West on:

- The fraction of incoming requests accepted for the promise and the wait before acceptance.
- Seven-day completion among accepted requests.
- Timely completion among all incoming requests, with subsequent outcomes tracked for those rejected or abandoned.

Standardize each district to the same pooled incoming-request mix, report the district differences and their uncertainty, and retain the within-group results so an aggregate does not hide a particular access problem. For the access policy, use equal acceptance probabilities for comparable requests as the stated target; any permitted operational difference should be specified before judging results. Completion parity should be assessed alongside that access target, not substituted for it.

Finally, estimate the tool’s effect prospectively using randomized tool availability across suitable teams or periods, with the same contract and training conditions and a recorded decision policy. Compare all incoming requests in the assigned groups, so changes in acceptance remain part of the measured effect. If randomization is impractical, a concurrent comparison with detailed case information would improve the evidence, while leaving unmeasured differences as a limitation. This would allow the network to evaluate the tool’s contribution separately from workload composition and to judge customer access alongside completion.

The customer saw a deleted note’s content again, but the evidence shows that the mobile update was rejected and the primary server still held the deletion. “Resurrection” can therefore describe a real display or export problem without establishing that the authoritative server record was restored.

## What happened to each copy

An **epoch** is a server-controlled generation number for the note. A **revision** orders accepted edits within one generation. A **tombstone** is the retained record that the note has been deleted; it is not the note’s former content. Under version 2, deletion advances the epoch and removes the current content. A high revision within an earlier epoch cannot override that deletion. [B11-S1]

| Time | Evidence | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 09:00 | Phone synchronized epoch 4, revision 8 | The phone’s last known server version |
| 09:10 | Browser deletion produced tombstone epoch 5 | The server deleted N and advanced its generation |
| 09:30 | Phone displayed its epoch-4 draft as “pending sync” | Local content was visible while disconnected |
| 09:40 | Mobile update returned 409 | That update was rejected |
| 09:41 | CSV included the draft title | Local export included retained draft content |
| 09:42 | Server GET returned 404 with tombstone epoch 5 | N remained deleted at this server read |

The trace comes from B11-S4. The offline display and export behavior are explained by the current interface specification, B11-S3.

## Why the handler rejects this update

The handler loads the stored note under a lock shared with deletion. Its **first** condition compares the request’s epoch 4 with the stored epoch 5. They differ, so it returns **409 immediately**. It never reaches the tombstone check or `write_content`. The phone’s local revision 9 does not alter that branch. [B11-S2]

The next branch, returning **410**, would reject an update supplying the current epoch while the stored note is still a tombstone. The final write happens only after both checks pass, and the server chooses the next revision as `stored.revision + 1`.

Because the shared lock covers the read, checks, and write, deletion cannot slip between a successful check and the write. If an update completes first, a later deletion removes it; if deletion completes first, the stale update encounters the newer epoch. This reasoning applies to the supplied mobile handler and deletion path.

The old timestamp sketch does not change that behavior. It is an earlier proposal, whereas the current contract and deployed code explicitly use epochs. Appearing first in search results gives the sketch no authority over the implemented rule. [B11-S1–S2]

## Why the CSV is not proof of restoration

There are three distinct claims: content reappeared on screen, content appeared in an exported file, and content became the primary server’s current note again. The first two occurred; the third is not supported by this trace.

After 409, the interface preserves the rejected draft in a conflict tray so the user can recover their work. The ordinary synchronized list excludes it, but the current CSV exporter reads local state and includes both kinds of item without a status column. A title in that CSV consequently cannot distinguish committed content from an uncommitted draft. The behavior under discussion has not yet been changed. [B11-S3]

The supported incident conclusion is specific: **this mobile request did not restore N, and the direct server read at 09:42 found N deleted**. It does not certify every possible writer or every moment in the system’s history.

## What a broader guarantee would require

To claim deletion cannot be bypassed anywhere, engineers would need to identify and review every path capable of writing note content or changing epochs and tombstones. That includes any administrative imports, backup restores, migrations, or direct database access that actually exist, plus the authorized explicit restore operation. They would need evidence that the relevant checks and concurrency protections apply consistently, with tests or stronger verification of those invariants. The packet supplies no such review, and the primary-service contract explicitly does not cover every administrative import tool. An intentional, authorized restore must also be distinguished from a stale update bypassing deletion. [B11-S1, B11-S4]

For the product, retain the recoverable draft but clarify its status. Once the app confirms the server deletion, show “Deleted on server; your unsynced draft is saved separately,” with a copy action. Default CSV exports could exclude conflict drafts, or include explicit status and source columns with a clear option to export them. Either change would address the customer’s understandable impression without presenting a rejected draft as a saved server note.

response:
The facts establish two successors with a shared psychological past and separate subsequent lives. They do not, by themselves, decide which criterion makes someone “the same person.” The community can nevertheless assign a clear practical obligation: East and West jointly owe **one completed map or one repayment**, because the supplied rule covers both authorized successors.

## Separate the questions

Several different relationships are being compressed into “same person”:

| Question | What would answer it? |
| --- | --- |
| Strict personal identity | A criterion for being one and the same individual over time |
| Psychological continuity | Connections through memory, intentions, abilities, and projects |
| Ownership | Rules determining who is entitled to particular property |
| Project obligation | Rules determining who must complete the work or repay |
| Blame | An account of an action, the agent’s involvement, and the conditions for holding them culpable |

Shared memories directly bear on psychological continuity. They do not automatically establish the other relationships. The technical report documents how the successors were produced, but supplies neither a test for metaphysical identity nor evidence that one successor has a privileged connection to Vale. [B12-S1]

This distinction also exposes a problem with saying that both successors are each **numerically identical** to Vale, meaning literally the same individual rather than merely similar. Under ordinary identity, if East is Vale and West is Vale, then East is West: identity is transitive. But East and West are stipulated to be distinct, independently acting successors with separate experiences. Both claims of strict identity therefore cannot stand together under that ordinary meaning. Psychological continuity can branch without being numerical identity.

## Which disagreements concern evidence, and which concern criteria?

East’s memory supports a connection to the promise, but cannot establish “I alone”: West has the same relevant memory. West is right about this symmetry of evidence. It does not follow that both are strictly Vale, or that neither is; that further judgment needs a criterion beyond the shared memory. East’s exclusive claim to the obligation also conflicts with the adopted community rule. [B12-S2–S3]

The spectator makes an unsupported prediction. Identical memories at the copying point do not guarantee identical future choices when new information and experience can differ. East has already received information West lacks. That fact does not tell us exactly what either will choose, but it defeats the claim that their shared past proves their futures must match. [B12-S1–S2]

The neighbor and treasurer make claims about how obligations should follow succession. The neighbor’s objection to two debts agrees with the rule’s limit of one performance or repayment. The treasurer instead assumes that an obligation must disappear unless a successor is strictly the original. That is an additional normative premise—an assumption about how obligations ought to work—and the actual rule rejects it by assigning obligations through authorized succession. Neither claim is settled merely by inspecting copied memories.

The proposed theories likewise select different criteria or priorities. Theory A requires one continuous physical implementation; memory resemblance alone cannot meet that requirement. If both successors count as new implementations, neither qualifies under that reading. Theory B emphasizes enough psychological continuity to sustain projects, allowing that valuable relationship to branch without necessarily calling both successors numerically identical to Vale. Theory C gives public recognition a constitutive role in identity, but would need a fuller account of which practices matter and how they handle branching. The adopted obligation rule cannot simply be treated as that account, because it expressly leaves metaphysical identity open. [B12-S3–S4]

The brochure’s “you live twice” supplies no argument for resolving these alternatives. Vale’s earlier cartography award supplies no evidence about identity after copying or the reach of the community rule. [B12-S4]

## What the community may require

Vale’s documented continuity plan named both East and West, so both meet the rule’s definition of an authorized successor. For the continued paid project, they jointly owe one completed map or one full repayment of the advance. They may agree how to divide the work or repayment. The rule does not prescribe equal halves or make either successor exclusively liable. Once the community receives the required map or repayment, it cannot demand another merely because there are two successors. [B12-S3]

This answers the project question even if the seminar remains divided about identity. It does not prove a theory of personhood, award either successor unrelated property, or authorize punishment. Ownership of other assets would require additional facts and rules.

## Later blame requires a new inquiry

If one successor later acts wrongly, assessing blame requires facts about that successor’s conduct, knowledge, intentions, and control, together with a defensible standard of responsibility. The other successor does not automatically inherit blame through a shared original or memories formed before the act. Neither even has access to the other’s later memories. [B12-S1]

Further facts could make both responsible—for example, if they knowingly planned an act together or one deliberately assisted the other. Any such conclusion would rest on their participation and the applicable moral rule, not on copying alone. The community’s assignment of one unfinished project establishes an obligation to perform; it provides no general rule for transferring blame between successors.

response:
Adding A increases one upstream component; it does not ensure that Q reaches a compartment where it can produce light. The experiments support several parts of that explanation, but they do not establish the complete working model or identify a single bottleneck.

### Separate the four things being measured

Under the laboratory's working model, light requires a connected sequence: E uses charged C to make Q; R carries Q across an intact membrane; and L consumes Q inside the compartment when local acidity is below the threshold. A increases E after a delay, without directly supplying the other conditions. This is the proposed mechanism against which to interpret the experiments, not an independently proved account of every step. [B01-S1]

Four distinctions matter:

- **Production:** More E protein means more enzyme is present, not necessarily that it converts P faster. Its activity also depends on conditions such as charged C.
- **Location:** Whole-cell Q includes Q on both sides of the membrane. A large total does not show that Q has reached L.
- **Consumption:** Q is an intermediate that can be used up. Its measured amount reflects accumulation after production and consumption, rather than measuring production alone.
- **Final readout:** Light reports a downstream result. An increase in E or Q does not by itself establish that every required step is working. [B01-S1]

### What the cultures show

At minute twenty, A-treated cultures had four times the E abundance and substantially more whole-cell Q than untreated cultures, but light changed only from 8 to 9. Adding the cofactor-charging treatment increased Q further, from 38 to 75, while light reached 10. These observations fit an explanation in which upstream supply increases but some downstream condition still restricts light. They do not directly measure E's reaction rate or locate the accumulated Q. The results are means from three cultures without uncertainty estimates, so the small light differences cannot confidently be distinguished from experimental variation. [B01-S2]

After M, Q fell from 38 to 17 while light rose from 9 to 31. This does **not** prove that E became less active. Better delivery of Q could let L consume it faster, leaving less Q present even while more light-producing product is made. Simply moving Q across the membrane would not lower the whole-cell total, because that assay counts both locations. The fall indicates a net decrease in the measured Q pool; relocation alone cannot explain that decrease. [B01-S1; B01-S2]

M's separate transport assay strengthens the transport explanation. However, that assay did not measure local acidity, so it does not establish that transport was M's only relevant effect. Unchanged E abundance also does not guarantee unchanged E activity. Increased consumption, reduced production, or both remain possible contributors to the falling Q pool. [B01-S2]

### Why the apparently decisive experiments remain ambiguous

Deleting R eliminated light, but the deletion also damaged the membrane. The experiment therefore shows that this combined disruption prevents light under the tested conditions; it does not isolate R's transport function as the cause. Failure of Q supplied outside the compartment to rescue those cultures cannot distinguish failed entry from consequences of membrane damage. [B01-S3]

Supplying Q inside intact isolated compartments produced light below the acidity threshold without A, and little light above it. This supports a downstream capacity to use internally supplied Q and shows that A is unnecessary for that result in this preparation. It also gives a direct reason to keep acidity in the explanation. But isolation removes soluble proteins and supplies charged C, so the experiment does not reproduce all the requirements of a whole cell or independently establish L as the sole responsible enzyme. [B01-S3]

Similarly, restoring R would be an ambiguous rescue if it also repaired the membrane: restored light could follow from restored transport, restored integrity, or both. The supplier's satisfaction score adds no evidence about any of these mechanisms. [B01-S3; B01-S4]

### A small set of experiments to separate the explanations

1. **Measure Q production and use over time, with its location resolved.** Compare A alone, A plus cofactor charging, and A plus M. Measure P-to-Q conversion directly, charged C, Q inside and outside the compartment, and light. If production remains steady while Q is consumed faster and light rises after M, that supports increased downstream use. If P-to-Q conversion falls, reduced production contributes. Location measurements would show whether A mainly builds an outside pool that cannot reach L.

2. **Vary transport and acidity separately while checking membrane integrity.** Measure transport and local acidity in the same preparations, then compare increased transport at controlled acidity with lowered acidity at comparable transport. More light after improved transport at fixed permissive acidity supports a transport constraint. More light after lowering acidity while transport is unchanged supports an acidity constraint. If both changes are required, both stages limit output; neither can be dismissed as irrelevant.

3. **Separate R restoration from membrane repair.** Test the proposed R rescue while measuring both transport and integrity, and, if feasible, compare it with an independent membrane repair. If integrity is restored but transport and light still require R, that strengthens the specific transport explanation. If repair restores light without R, R is not indispensable under those rescue conditions. A rescue that restores everything together would leave the original ambiguity unresolved. Repeat these comparisons with uncertainty estimates so that apparent differences can be judged against culture-to-culture variation.

response:
The reports address different questions, so their results need not contradict one another. Together they suggest that Luma can reduce heat entering through a roof under some conditions, but they do **not establish that it improves comfort in the town's actual housing**, especially during humid evenings in top-floor apartments.

### What was assigned or selected, and what was measured?

| Report | How the comparison was formed | What was measured | What it can support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Randomized pilot | Twenty buildings were assigned to coatings by chance | Average afternoon indoor temperature; a comfort questionnaire with incomplete responses | The strongest available comparison for attributing an afternoon temperature difference to Luma |
| Contractor comparison | Owners chose coating, other improvements, and survey participation | Reported afternoons of discomfort | An association between the voluntarily coated group and fewer reported discomfort afternoons |
| Chamber experiment | Six paired panels were compared under controlled conditions | Inward heat flow | A physical effect under the tested roof material and chamber conditions |

These differences matter because heat flow, room temperature, and residents' comfort are related but distinct outcomes. A percentage change in one is not automatically the same percentage change in another. [B02-S1–S3]

### The pilot is uncertain, not a demonstration of no effect

The pilot's estimate was **0.6 temperature units cooler** with Luma. Its cluster-adjusted uncertainty interval ran from 1.4 units cooler to 0.2 units warmer. Here, “cluster-adjusted” means the analysis accounts for apartments belonging to the same building and sharing conditions. The interval includes no difference, but also includes potentially useful cooling; crossing zero does not establish that the true effect is zero. [B02-S1]

The coating was assigned to 20 buildings, not independently to 740 apartments. Apartments under the same roof share exposure and ventilation, so counting all of them as separate experimental assignments exaggerates how much independent information the trial contains. The later analyst's narrower interval therefore does not overturn the building-level analysis. More apartment measurements can improve information about a building, but they do not create additional independently assigned buildings. [B02-S1]

The comfort evidence has a separate problem: questionnaire responses came from 78% of control occupants but only 51% of treated occupants. If respondents differed from nonrespondents in comfort, comparing respondents could give a misleading picture. The direction of that distortion is unknown because reasons for nonresponse are missing. Occupants also knew their coating, which could affect subjective reports. Neither issue proves that the reports are wrong; both limit what can be concluded from them. The packet supplies no comfort scores from which to calculate a reliable benefit. [B02-S1]

### The contractor's larger sample does not isolate Luma

The contractor reports 30% fewer discomfort afternoons in coated buildings. But external shades were installed in 70% of those buildings versus 15% of uncoated buildings. Luma and shade installation therefore travel together in this comparison, and the analysis adjusted only for building age. Insulation, neighborhood, previous discomfort, and who elected to participate after hearing complaints could also explain part of the difference. [B02-S2]

A larger sample can reduce random fluctuation without removing these systematic differences. Calling the pilot underpowered—too small to reliably distinguish some plausible effects—does not make the contractor's estimate causal. Nor can the committee translate the relative 30% difference into an absolute number of afternoons saved without the underlying counts and definitions. [B02-S2]

### The chamber supplies a mechanism, with transfer limits

The 18% reduction in inward heat flow supports a physical benefit in the six paired panels under fixed radiation, equal airflow, dry surfaces, and no internal heat sources. It does not validate the contractor's 30% comfort estimate: it measures a different outcome in a different setting. [B02-S3]

Only one of the town's three common roof materials was tested. The wet-surface estimate was 3%, but absent replication and uncertainty information, its precision and the strength of the difference from the dry result cannot be assessed. A wet surface is also not interchangeable with a humid evening. The available methods and numerical results allow scrutiny; manufacturer funding alone neither establishes nor defeats the findings. The design award supplies no evidence about heat or comfort. [B02-S3; B02-S4]

### What would answer the committee's question?

The main applicability gap is specific: most local complaints concern top-floor apartments during humid evenings, whereas the pilot measured average afternoon temperature and half its buildings were outside town in a drier area. Even a more precise estimate for that pilot would not automatically establish the effect in the housing and conditions the committee cares about. [B02-S1; B02-S4]

The most valuable next study would randomly assign **local buildings** to Luma or the existing coating and follow them over the same summer period. It should include the town's three roof materials and relevant housing types, record other improvements such as shades, and make top-floor comfort during humid evenings a specified outcome before results are examined. Repeated temperature and humidity measurements would connect physical changes to repeated resident comfort assessments. Consistent follow-up of residents and an analysis of missing responses would address the current questionnaire gap. [B02-S1–S4]

The analysis should retain the building as the unit of assignment and explain whether its average represents buildings or apartments, since buildings vary greatly in size. The study needs enough buildings to distinguish a benefit the committee would consider worthwhile, rather than simply a large count of apartments.

A modest overall average could conceal a larger benefit for the hottest apartments—or no benefit for them. That possibility calls for a planned comparison using apartments identified as hot before treatment, not a favorable subgroup selected afterward. The present packet supplies no such result. A local randomized study focused on the relevant time, residents, and roof materials would address both attribution and applicability; merely enlarging the contractor's selected sample would leave those gaps in place.

Under the enacted rules supplied here, **Alder requires an inspection certificate; Birch can use a transition declaration; Cedar's position depends first on where its workshop lies and, if it is in Port Meridian, on what the warehouse delivery actually represented.** A document's later publication date does not by itself change the governing rule.

### Which documents control?

The enacted ordinance establishes eligibility. The implementing office can specify forms, so its circular governs the declaration's required evidence and filing process, but it cannot move the ordinance's eligibility dates. The informal training slide is an incomplete summary: “orders received” cannot replace a signed purchase agreement, and its omission of physical delivery does not remove that condition. [B03-S1; B03-S2]

The May 28 amendment is explicitly a proposal requiring a separate council vote. The packet records no enactment or promulgation. The June 3 digest links only to that proposal, so its confident phrase “June extension” supplies no basis for applying a June 15 cutoff. The modernization brochure has no bearing on eligibility. [B03-S3]

The relevant dates perform different jobs:

| Date or event | What it determines |
| --- | --- |
| April 2 publication | The ordinance's publication date and the dividing date for eligible signed agreements: the agreement must be earlier than April 2 |
| June 1 commencement | The certificate requirement begins for commercial equipment first placed into service in the port district from that date |
| Physical customer delivery before June 1 | A separate condition for the transition alternative; warehouse arrival, dispatch, customs clearance, and invoicing do not substitute for it |
| First operation | When the equipment enters service; this is distinct from delivery and filing |
| July 15 filing limit | The last date for filing a qualifying declaration; it does not extend the agreement or delivery conditions |

The circular expressly allows filing after first use when the substantive transition conditions were met. [B03-S1; B03-S2]

### Alder: certificate required

Alder's March 29 signed agreement satisfies the agreement condition. Its physical delivery to the Port Meridian customer on June 3 does **not** satisfy delivery before June 1. Arrival at the port warehouse on May 29 cannot replace the stated customer-delivery date. Because Alder first operated commercially in Port Meridian on June 5, it falls under the certificate requirement and cannot use the documented transition alternative. [B03-S1; B03-S4]

The draft does not change that answer. Furthermore, its proposed extension concerns dock-repair delays, and the packet does not establish that Alder experienced such a delay. The packet also does not say whether Alder already has an inspection certificate: it establishes the requirement, not an actual certificate violation. [B03-S3; B03-S4]

### Birch: eligible for a transition declaration

Birch meets both substantive conditions: its signed agreement is dated April 1, before April 2, and its customer received it physically on May 31, before June 1. Its June 2 first use does not remove that eligibility. [B03-S1; B03-S4]

The July 10 appointment is within the July 15 filing period, and filing after first use is expressly permitted. Birch can therefore use the transition route, provided a complete declaration is actually filed on time with the signed agreement, proof of physical customer delivery, and serial number. An appointment is not proof that filing has occurred or that the documents are complete. [B03-S2; B03-S4]

### Cedar: two facts need checking

**First, establish the workshop's district.** Cedar first operated commercially on June 4, but the workshop's district assignment and the boundary map are missing. A warehouse postal address reading “Meridian Bay” does not establish where the workshop is situated within the legal district boundaries. [B03-S4]

- If the workshop is outside Port Meridian, this ordinance imposes no certificate requirement on that first use. Any rules for the district concerned must be checked separately; the packet does not provide Estuary's regime.
- If the workshop is inside Port Meridian, the June 4 first use brings Cedar within this ordinance, subject to the transition alternative. [B03-S1]

**Second, if Port Meridian's rules apply, establish physical customer delivery.** The March 20 agreement qualifies. But “delivered May 25 to a warehouse” does not say whether that was delivery to the customer or merely intermediate storage. [B03-S4]

If the customer physically received Cedar there on May 25—or otherwise received it before June 1—it can use a transition declaration, with the required evidence and timely filing. If physical customer delivery occurred on or after June 1, it needs an inspection certificate. Until the recipient and delivery date are established, the transition decision remains open. [B03-S1; B03-S2]

The team's decision process should therefore start with use and district, identify the governing enacted rule, then check the agreement and physical customer-delivery facts separately. Only after eligibility is established should the team check forms and filing. Publication dates help identify documents; they do not give an informal summary or an unenacted draft authority to change the ordinance.

The trial shows **less expired stock and higher contribution across the two stores**, but it does not establish better demand forecasts or preserved customer service. The same totals could arise from improved matching, underordering at North, changed customer demand, or directing more stock toward South's new customer.

### What the arithmetic establishes

Because opening and closing stock were zero and transfers were prohibited, each store's receipts equal sales plus discards. The ledger therefore accounts for all supplied items. [B04-S1]

| Store | Items received: baseline → trial | Items sold: baseline → trial | Items discarded: baseline → trial | Hours without stock: baseline → trial |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| North | 1,000 → 800 | 900 → 760 | 100 → 40 | 2 → 18 |
| South | 400 → 600 | 360 → 570 | 40 → 30 | 1 → 1 |
| Total | 1,400 → 1,400 | 1,260 → 1,330 | 140 → 70 | 3 → 19 |

Using those counts, expired waste fell by 70 items, or **50% relative to the original 140**. Since total receipts stayed at 1,400, the discarded share also halved, from 10% to 5%. That is a five-percentage-point decrease. It is not a measurement of forecast accuracy: the packet supplies neither forecasts nor a complete measure of the demand those forecasts were meant to predict. [B04-S1]

Sales divided by receipts rose from 90% to 95%, both at each store and overall. This measures the share of supplied stock that sold. It does not measure the share of customers whose requests were fulfilled. Ordering fewer items can raise that ratio while leaving more customers unable to buy. [B04-S1; B04-S2]

North was without stock for 1% of opening hours before the trial and 9% during it. South remained at 0.5%. Across 400 store-hours per period, time without stock rose from 0.75% to 4.75%. These are availability measures, not percentages of disappointed customers: one busy hour can involve many more purchase attempts than another. Nevertheless, North's worsening availability directly challenges an unqualified claim that service was preserved. [B04-S2]

### Contribution increased by 700 currency units

Contribution here is sales revenue minus the acquisition cost of **all items received**, including those that expired:

\[
\text{Contribution}=10\times\text{items sold}-6\times\text{items received}.
\]

| Store | Baseline contribution | Trial contribution | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| North | 3,000 | 2,800 | −200 |
| South | 1,200 | 2,100 | +900 |
| Total | **4,200** | **4,900** | **+700** |

For example, trial contribution is \(10(1,330)-6(1,400)=4,900\). Aggregate revenue rose from 12,600 to 13,300, while aggregate acquisition cost remained 8,400. Contribution therefore rose by 700, approximately 16.7% of the baseline contribution. Disposal cost and other unchanged expenses are excluded as requested; their unknown amounts prevent calculating the absolute result after those expenses. These calculations follow from the ledger and prices, not from an attribution of the gain to the forecasting system. [B04-S1]

### Several causal stories fit the evidence

**Better matching is possible.** The system may have reduced excess supply at North and increased supply where South could sell it. But the intervention coincided with changes that could produce the same observed pattern. North lost a nearby bus stop, potentially changing customer numbers and arrival times; South acquired a cafeteria customer that bought 120 items. Weather and events also changed. Both stores adopted together, leaving no contemporary comparison showing what would have happened without the system. [B04-S3]

**North may have ordered too little, or received stock at the wrong times.** Its receipts fell by 200 and sales fell by 140 while stockout hours increased. More time without stock does not prove total demand rose: lower supply or a different timing of demand can produce more shortages even if total demand is unchanged or lower. The two notes about long queues suggest pressure at particular moments, but cannot establish demand over four weeks. [B04-S1; B04-S2]

**South's new business may explain some of the aggregate improvement.** Its sales rose by 210, with 120 trial sales identified as cafeteria purchases. The remaining 450 sales exceed baseline sales by 90, but that residual is not an estimate of the system's effect. Nor can we assume the cafeteria's purchases would simply subtract from an otherwise unchanged store: its presence may have affected ordering and availability. [B04-S1; B04-S3]

Finally, selecting stores because waste was unusually high makes a subsequent decline less decisive. An unusually bad period may be followed by a more ordinary one without an effective intervention. The marketing statement about predictability supplies no evidence about these stores. [B04-S2; B04-S3]

### What is missing about demand?

Demand here means the purchases customers would have wanted to make if the item had been available under the relevant trading conditions. Completed sales record only the fulfilled part.

Stockout durations do not reveal how many purchase attempts occurred during them, how many shoppers substituted, or how many returned later. The records therefore cannot supply a numerical estimate of unmet demand, establish a positive minimum for lost purchases, or provide a useful upper bound. Multiplying stockout hours by the average sales rate would require an unsupported assumption that demand during unavailable hours resembled demand during available hours. The queue notes do not repair that gap. [B04-S2]

Because training used sales rather than attempted purchases, the system may learn that stock-limited periods had low demand. That is a possible mechanism for repeated underordering, not proof that it happened here. [B04-S3]

### A feasible next evaluation

Expand as a controlled trial: assign comparable stores to the system or existing practice by chance, run both groups over the same periods, and include stores with different customer patterns. Record new contracts, transport disruptions, and other changes. Avoid choosing only stores coming off exceptionally high waste.

Alongside receipts, expiry, revenue, and costs, collect purchase attempts, unavailable-item requests, substitutions, and the timing of stockouts. Define success beforehand as lower waste or higher contribution **with an acceptable level of fulfilled demand**, and assess results separately for customer patterns such as regular contract orders and walk-in trade.

Lower waste with stable fulfillment would support improved matching. Lower waste accompanied by more unfilled requests would reveal underordering. Gains concentrated in newly contracted demand would limit the case for expansion to other store types.

Even a successful reconstruction of all past demand would answer only how much demand existed. It would not establish what ordering, waste, service, and contribution would have been without the system. The contemporary randomized comparison is what addresses that causal question.

The archive most strongly supports **a practical naming practice among some traders that officials recorded alongside household identities**. It also preserves a later political interpretation of those names. It does not establish that resistance was their chief purpose, that officials created the practice, or that the same explanation applies to all residents.

### The strongest evidence concerns trade and administration

The harbor register shows that a later hand added night names beside 19 of the 62 surviving household-name entries. Thirteen of those 19 traders operated boats after dusk. That association supports a connection with river work, although the six entries without recorded boat occupations cannot simply be classified as non-boat workers. The marginal instruction links short names to the tide and household names to taxation, suggesting that the two identifiers could serve different practical purposes. [B05-S1]

The register also demonstrates administrative recording: someone made room for both names within a tax-related document. But recording a practice is different from inventing it or making it a formal category throughout the town. The annotations are undated, and the note and names have not been attributed to the same clerk. They therefore cannot be treated as one securely dated naming policy. [B05-S1]

The year 44 merchants' letter gives the clearest evidence of a stated practical intention. Four traders complain that inspectors' requests for household names and boatmen's use of water names delay the barley, then ask the clerk to keep both. Their explicit aim is faster clearance through recognition of both identifiers. Three signatories match annotated register entries, connecting this complaint with some of the people visible there. The fourth's absence from the surviving register proves little because the register is incomplete. [B05-S2]

This makes trading convenience and administrative recognition complementary possibilities: a name useful among boatmen could become an administrative problem when inspectors use a different identifier, and recording both could resolve that problem.

The official-copy problem remains real but limited. A clerk might have softened confrontational language, as the historian proposes. Without an independent version, however, that possibility cannot supply political statements missing from the surviving petition. The letter supports its stated request more strongly than an inferred hidden agenda. [B05-S2]

### Resistance is a supported interpretation, but a weaker account of the original purpose

The watch officer's memoir explicitly presents night names as frustrating official control and associates them with youthful mockery of the ledgers. It therefore supplies evidence that naming could be remembered and represented as resistance. It may also preserve a real recollection of earlier confrontation. [B05-S3]

Several limits prevent treating it as decisive testimony about traders' chief motives in year 43. It was written in year 79, 36 years later; the author acknowledges a memory error elsewhere; and the book was sold during a campaign against a new tax authority. Those circumstances give reason to examine both memory and political presentation. They do not prove fabrication. Accurate descriptions of three gates corroborate his geographical knowledge, not the separate story about naming or what traders intended. [B05-S3]

The song fragment supplies still less direct evidence about historical behavior. Its imagery permits a reading in which different names accompany different settings or aspects of life. Nothing says that one identity replaced the other, and “at home I buried neither” fits continued coexistence better than the later catalog's claim of abandonment. But a poetic speaker is not a survey of actual residents. [B05-S4]

The year 88 date belongs to the surviving copy, not necessarily to the song's composition. The collector's resistance heading is an interpretation, weakened by the inclusion of unrelated wedding verses. The year 112 catalog is evidence of a later interpretation, not contemporary testimony that citizens discarded household identities. [B05-S4]

### Function, intention, and later use can differ

A naming practice can help people identify one another in trade, create difficulty for inspectors, and later become a symbol of resistance. Those functions can coexist without every participant intending all of them.

The letter establishes that its petitioners wanted a practical administrative change. The register shows official accommodation in particular entries. The memoir presents obstruction and mockery. None of these establishes one shared motive across traders, officials, and other residents. Later political uses do not erase an earlier practical role, and an earlier practical role does not rule out contemporary acts of resistance. [B05-S1–S4]

The strongest defensible synthesis for the museum is therefore that **night names served as alternative identifiers in the river-trading world visible in these records; their interaction with household-based taxation created both practical friction and opportunities for political interpretation**. The trade and administrative functions have the strongest direct support. Resistance remains credible as one use or meaning, but the archive does not establish it as the chief origin or purpose.

One live alternative is that deliberate evasion or mockery already accompanied ordinary trading use in the early period, while the official petition emphasized an acceptable practical complaint. The memoir and the letter's description of delays make that possible. They do not establish the suppressed wording or participants' intentions needed to make it the leading conclusion.

The selected archive cannot tell us how common night names were among all residents, when they began, or whether practical, administrative, and resistant uses followed a single sequence. Nineteen annotated entries out of 62 surviving entries describe this incomplete register, not town-wide prevalence. Undated annotations and an undated song composition also prevent a secure chronology of the practice. Claims about a town-wide motive would go beyond the surviving evidence. [B05-S1–S4]

这次事件说明：**有效签名可以让网关确认请求来自一个已识别的客户，并检查签名所覆盖的内容是否被修改；它既不赋予客户任意租户的权限，也不保证同一笔业务只执行一次。** 重复订单符合 version 3 的已知行为，不能据此认定 HMAC 被破解。[B06-S1; B06-S3]

### 三种检查分别回答什么问题？

| 检查 | 在本事件中回答的问题 | 当前实现 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 身份认证 | 这个请求能否通过某个已识别客户的密钥验证？ | 网关验证签名，并添加 `X-Client-ID` |
| 授权 | 这个客户是否有权在目标租户执行操作？ | 服务调用 `directory.is_member(client, tenant)`；不属于该租户则返回 `403` |
| 重放防护 | 这次带有有效凭据的请求是否已经提交过？ | version 3 没有保存已使用请求标识的 nonce store，也不承诺最多执行一次 |

当前签名计算为：

```text
HMAC_SHA256(secret, method + "\n" + path + "\n" + timestamp + "\n" + SHA256(body_bytes))
```

因此，`method`、`path`、`timestamp` 和 `body_bytes` 都与签名关联。时间戳必须与网关时间相差不超过 60 秒，但同一份请求在这段时间内可以多次满足条件。时间戳检查限制的是请求的新旧程度，不能识别“这笔订单是否已经创建”。本事件所有密钥都允许 `POST`，所以方法限制不能解释两条租户路径的不同结果。[B06-S1]

### 四次响应分别说明了什么？

| 时间与请求 | 观察到的结果 | 能得出的结论及其边界 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10:00:08：首次提交 `POST /tenants/T1/orders` | 网关接受，服务返回 `201`，随后响应连接失败 | 请求通过认证；K 属于 T1，代码执行到 `save_order(tenant, order)` 后返回。连接失败不表示订单被撤销，也不表示服务没有处理请求。 |
| 10:00:15：重试相同的方法、路径、时间戳、请求体和签名 | 再次返回 `201`；存储日志显示 T1 中两个不同订单标识都对应 R7 | 原时间戳仍在 60 秒窗口内，同一签名再次通过。两个 `201` 本身不足以证明重复创建；这里是存储日志进一步证实了两个订单。 |
| 10:00:20：把捕获的路径改成 `/tenants/T2/orders`，未重新签名 | 网关在转发前拒绝 | 修改后的路径与原签名不匹配。这展示了该次路径篡改被拦截，没有测试服务的租户成员检查。 |
| 10:00:25：K 使用合法密钥为 T2 路径重新计算有效签名 | 网关接受，服务返回 `403` | K 能证明自己的身份，但 K 不是 T2 成员。代码在解析请求体和调用 `save_order(tenant, order)` 之前拒绝。签名没有创造租户成员资格。 |

这些结论来自给定时间线和代码；目录查询在这些时刻准确，且该部署的服务只能经网关访问。[B06-S2; B06-S3]

首次请求的请求体是 `{"reference":"R7","amount":40}`。当前服务没有针对 `order.reference` 的唯一性检查、幂等键处理或跨重试共享的事务标识。因此，第二次提交没有在所示代码中被识别为同一笔业务。日志证明这一次确实重复创建，但不能据此推断 `save_order` 对所有输入都没有任何未公开的去重行为。[B06-S2; B06-S3]

### 团队争论中，哪些文档适用？

应以当前 version 3 契约解释这个部署。version 1 关于请求不能重复的说明依赖于一个已被移除的 nonce 数据库，不能当作当前保证。幻灯片把“签名有效”和“有权访问资源”合并了，遗漏了契约要求服务独立执行的授权检查。99.99 percent availability 描述可用性，不能证明租户隔离或去重正确。[B06-S1; B06-S4]

重复提交的是一份原本有效的请求，并没有伪造签名，所以重复订单不证明 HMAC 失效。反过来，一次篡改被拒绝也不能证明整个实现不存在其他安全问题。这份材料只支持对所列请求及相关代码路径的判断。

### 租户授权应放在哪里？

**保留并完善服务端、业务操作之前的授权检查。** 网关负责按当前契约识别客户，服务根据 `X-Client-ID` 和路径中的 `tenant`，检查成员资格及该操作需要的资源权限。把租户写进已签名的 `path`，只是把请求绑定到这个目标；是否允许访问这个目标，仍由授权规则决定。[B06-S1; B06-S2]

所示代码已经执行成员检查，但材料没有展示其他资源权限规则，不能把这段代码称为完整实现了所有资源授权。后续加入重试结果缓存时，也应先检查当前调用者的权限，再返回该租户的既有结果。

### 建议的重试设计：为同一笔业务保存同一份结果

以下是建议改动，不是当前已有保证。目标是实现“幂等”：客户端因为未收到响应而重试时，服务返回同一笔业务的结果，不再创建另一个订单。

1. **客户端为每笔创建操作生成稳定的操作标识。** 同一笔业务重试时沿用它，另一笔业务使用不同标识。重试可以使用新的 `timestamp` 和签名，操作标识仍不变。应把标识纳入受签名保护的内容，例如请求体；若使用新增请求头，就需要明确扩展签名契约，因为当前公式不会自动覆盖任意新头。

2. **服务按客户、租户和操作标识保存处理记录。** 同时记录方法、目标路径、业务内容摘要及最终响应。相同标识对应相同内容时，返回已保存的订单标识和结果；相同标识却改变金额或其他业务内容时，应按明确规则拒绝，不能悄悄当成另一笔订单。

3. **把创建订单与记录结果作为一个不可分割的提交。** 如果数据存储支持事务，可在同一事务内完成，并用唯一性约束协调并发重试。这样，两个同时到达的请求不能分别创建订单。尚在处理的重试可以等待或查询状态；已经提交但响应丢失的重试应得到原结果。不能先创建订单，再依赖一个可能失败的独立步骤记录“已处理”。

4. **明确记录保存多久，以及过期后怎么办。** 保存期限应覆盖承诺支持的重试周期，不能直接照搬 60 秒时间窗口。若删除记录后仍允许旧操作标识重新执行，就不能继续保证该操作不会重复；必须定义过期拒绝、查询原订单或其他明确行为。

`order.reference` 目前没有唯一性保证。只有在业务规则明确规定某个范围内的参考号必须唯一时，才适合把这种约束也用于防止重复；不能仅因两笔订单都写着 R7，就假定现有契约已有该规则。[B06-S2]

“全局拒绝所有重复签名”不能单独解决这个重试问题：它可能挡住连接失败后的正常重试，却不给客户端原订单结果；同一业务换一个时间戳重新签名后，又会得到不同签名。若还要限制捕获请求的重复使用，可以另行设计带保存期限的 nonce 检查，但需要与业务操作标识分工：前者识别一次提交是否已出现，后者让同一笔业务的多次提交得到稳定结果。

事件证据最终能确定的是：这次 T1 重试产生了两个订单；未重新签名的路径修改被网关拦截；K 合法签名的 T2 请求被服务的成员检查拒绝。它没有证明所有重复请求都会产生重复订单，也没有证明任何未展示的权限路径或去重机制具有什么行为。[B06-S2; B06-S3]

Die Messwerte zeigen keine Energieerzeugung: Während der Entladung liefert der Speicher zusätzlich zum Strom Energie. Über den vollständigen Entlade- und Ladezyklus erhält der Raum **80 kWh Nutzwärme bei 110 kWh Stromverbrauch der Apparatur**. Der Nutzwirkungsgrad beträgt damit rund **72,7 %**. [B07-S1–S3]

### Leistung und Energie auseinanderhalten

**kW bezeichnet Leistung**, also wie schnell Energie übertragen wird. **kWh bezeichnet eine Energiemenge**. Eine durchschnittliche Leistung von 2 kW über 10 Stunden ergibt beispielsweise \(2\times10=20\) kWh. Deshalb darf man 2 kW nicht direkt zu 90 kWh addieren; zuerst muss die Leistung mit ihrer Betriebsdauer multipliziert werden. [B07-S2–S4]

Die folgende Bilanz gilt zunächst für die **Apparatur einschließlich Speicher**, ohne Überwachungscomputer. Die Speicheränderung ist positiv beim Laden und negativ beim Entladen. [B07-S1]

| Phase | Stromzufuhr | Nutzwärme im Raum | Speicheränderung | Wärmeverlust zum Flur |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Entladen, 10 Stunden | 20 kWh | 80 kWh | −70 kWh | 10 kWh |
| Laden, 5 Stunden | 90 kWh | 0 kWh | +70 kWh | 20 kWh |
| Vollständiger Zyklus | 110 kWh | 80 kWh | 0 kWh | 30 kWh |

Die Werte folgen aus den angegebenen mittleren Leistungen und Messungen. [B07-S2, B07-S3]

### Beide Phasen erfüllen die Energiebilanz

Beim Entladen stehen **20 kWh Strom plus 70 kWh abgegebene Speicherenergie** zur Verfügung. Diese insgesamt 90 kWh verlassen die Apparatur als 80 kWh Raumwärme und 10 kWh Flurwärme:

\[
20+70=80+10\quad\text{(jeweils kWh).}
\]

Der Temperaturabfall des Speichers bedeutet deshalb nicht, dass sämtliche Raumwärme allein aus ihm stammt: Seine gemessene Energieabnahme beträgt nur 70 kWh, während der Raum 80 kWh erhält. Die elektrische Zufuhr gehört ebenfalls zur Bilanz. Wie sich die beiden Energiequellen im Einzelnen auf Raumwärme und Verluste verteilen, sagen diese Gesamtmessungen nicht. [B07-S1, B07-S2]

Beim Laden werden 90 kWh Strom zugeführt. Davon erhöhen 70 kWh den Speicherinhalt; 20 kWh gelangen in den Flur:

\[
90=70+20\quad\text{(jeweils kWh).}
\]

Danach hat der Speicher wieder seinen Anfangszustand. Die Bezeichnung „Wartung“ ändert nichts daran, dass diese Ladephase für den nächsten gleichen Entladevorgang erforderlich ist. [B07-S3]

### Welche Kennzahl beantwortet welche Frage?

Die Rechnung des Verkäufers ist arithmetisch richtig:

\[
\frac{8\ \mathrm{kW}}{2\ \mathrm{kW}}
=\frac{80\ \mathrm{kWh}}{20\ \mathrm{kWh}}=4.
\]

Sie beschreibt das Verhältnis von Raumwärme zu gleichzeitig zugeführtem Strom **während der Entladephase**. Als Prozentzahl sind das 400 %. Als „Wirkungsgrad des Gesamtsystems“ ist die Bezeichnung jedoch irreführend, weil die verbrauchte Speicherenergie im Nenner fehlt. Auch der Kritiker irrt daher: Ein Wärmeausgang oberhalb der gleichzeitigen elektrischen Zufuhr widerspricht bei einem sich entladenden Speicher nicht der Energieerhaltung und beweist keinen Messfehler. [B07-S2, B07-S4]

Bezieht man die Speicherabnahme ein, erreichen beim Entladen \(80/(20+70)\approx88{,}9\,\%\) der verfügbaren Energie den Raum. Beim Laden bleiben \(70/90\approx77{,}8\,\%\) der zugeführten Energie im Speicher. Diese beiden Kennzahlen beschreiben unterschiedliche Phasen. Der vollständige Zyklus ergibt dagegen:

\[
\eta_\text{Raum, Apparatur}
=\frac{80}{20+90}
\approx72{,}7\,\%.

Die übrigen 30 kWh gehen in den Flur; netto bleibt keine zusätzliche Energie gespeichert. [B07-S2, B07-S3]
